snippet.title: BCCI: The Day Regulators Shut Down a Global Bank
snippet.description:
The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) was shut down on July 5, 1991, after regulators uncovered an extensive pattern of financial deception.

Across multiple countries, accounts were frozen, and customers who trusted the bank suddenly lost access to their money.

Founded in 1972 by Pakistani banker Agha Hassan Abedi, BCCI grew into an international banking empire operating in more than 70 countries. It served ordinary depositors, businesses, and wealthy investors while senior figures concealed financial losses, used offshore companies to obscure transactions, and secretly gained control of American banks.

This documentary investigates the rise and collapse of BCCI, from its connections to Middle Eastern wealth and its hidden acquisition of First American to the Gokal family's troubled loans and the bank's relationship with Panamanian leader Manuel Noriega.

We examine Operation SeaChase, which exposed money laundering connected to drug trafficking, the intelligence concerning BCCI's secret ownership of American banks, and the regulatory failures that allowed the institution to survive despite years of warning signs.

The investigation culminates in the Price Waterhouse Sandstorm Report and the coordinated closure of BCCI in July 1991.

But the consequences did not end when the bank closed. Depositors, employees, and small businesses faced years of financial uncertainty while courts and liquidators attempted to recover billions of dollars.

BCCI's history reveals how an institution built around international opportunity became a case study in financial fraud, political influence, secrecy, and the limits of banking regulation.

snippet.title: How To Use the Bank of America Card Lock Feature
snippet.description:
In this video, let's talk about how to use the Bank of America card lock feature. This feature allows you to instantly freeze your debit or credit card, which is a quick way to protect your money if your card is lost or you notice suspicious activity.

To use it, head over to your card settings within the Bank of America app or website. Where you find it will depend on whether you have a debit card linked to a checking account or a credit card account.

Once you're in the manage cards section, open the card settings for the specific card you want to lock. There, you'll see the option called lock your card, so simply toggle it on to freeze the card instantly.

When you want to use the card again, just come back to the same setting and toggle it off, and your card will be unlocked right away. That's the way to do this. If this video was helpful to you, be sure to subscribe, and I'll see you in the next one.

snippet.title: How To Fix Bank of America Cannot Enable Zelle Limit !
snippet.description:
In this video, let's talk about how to fix Bank of America cannot enable Zelle limit. The key thing to know is that within the Bank of America platform, you won't find an option that lets you manually toggle the Zelle limit on or off, since all Zelle limits are automatically determined by various factors.

For example, if your account is new, you'll generally have a lower limit. However, if your account is older than 60 days, you should normally have a daily limit of around $3,500. Your account and client classifications also matter, so consumer checking accounts typically allow around $3,500 per day or $20,000 per month, while small business checking accounts may go up to $15,000 per day.

These limits are also based on the automated behavior risk score that Bank of America assigns, which factors in your past transaction history as well as your average available balance. So the safer and more consistent your banking activity, the better your limits are likely to be.

There's no manual switch to enable or increase the limit, so the best approach is to keep your account in good standing and let Bank of America adjust your limit over time. That's the way it works. If this video was helpful to you, be sure to subscribe.

snippet.description:
Bank Of America $1.21B Fine: Only $35.59 Per $100K?

Bank of America's $1.21 billion fine (widely reported as the Bank of America $1.2 billion fine) sounds historic, until you compare it to the bank's roughly $3.4 trillion in assets. Here is how America's second-largest bank failed to report on time more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, and why the penalty works out to about $35.59 per $100,000.

On October 13, 2026, the U.S. Treasury announced more than $1.21 billion in penalties against Bank of America across three agencies: FinCEN ($1.2 billion), the OCC (a record $750 million, credited toward the FinCEN amount) and OFAC ($11.6 million for 475 apparent sanctions violations). In this Debtloom breakdown we cover how the bank admitted willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act, why regulators say it failed to fix its December 2024 cease and desist order, how the fine compares with about $6.9 billion in third quarter net income, the American Express $350 million penalty from October 8, 2026, and the questions around lawsuits and a possible criminal investigation.

snippet.title: How To Use Bank of America SafeBalance Feature !
snippet.description:
In today's video, let's talk about how to use Bank of America's Safe Balance feature. The good news is you don't need to manually turn it on, since it's automatically enabled within your account once you have the right account type.

Safe Balance is essentially a fee-protected account, meaning if you go over your spending limit, Bank of America does not charge you the NSF fee, which is the non-sufficient funds or overdraft fee that other accounts typically charge.

So if you attempt to make a purchase using your debit card, or even try to pay online, and the cost is more than your available balance, Bank of America will simply decline the transaction. Because the transaction is declined, your account is prevented from dropping below zero.

This means you never have to worry about unexpected overdraft charges piling up. The feature is already available within the platform, so there's nothing extra to set up. If this video did help you out, be sure to subscribe, and I'll see you in the next one.

snippet.title: Who Invented the Credit Card?
snippet.description:
When was the credit card invented? The first general-purpose charge card, Diners Club, arrived in 1950, and the first mass-market bank credit card, BankAmericard (today's Visa), launched in 1958, when Bank of America mailed about 60,000 cards to Fresno. Who invented the credit card? No single person: Brooklyn banker John Biggins created "Charg-It" in 1946, Diners Club made the idea famous, and Joseph Williams designed BankAmericard.

You've probably heard the story: a businessman forgets his wallet at a fancy New York dinner and invents the credit card so it never happens again. The man who wrote that story for the company later admitted he made it up.

The real story is stranger. A bank mailed sixty thousand credit cards to a whole city without asking anyone. Some cards ended up with dogs. And a court case is the reason your card bill probably comes from a state you've never visited.

🪙 Before plastic: department-store charge coins, metal name plates, and a Brooklyn banker's "Charg-It"
🍽️ The forgotten wallet: the most famous origin story in finance, written by a press agent
📬 The Fresno Drop: about 60,000 unasked-for cards in one go; more than one in five accounts fell behind
🐶 The flood: millions of cards mailed to people who never asked (including, reportedly, dogs), until Congress banned it
⚖️ The court case: the Supreme Court said a bank follows its own state's interest rules, wherever you live
🏛️ South Dakota: in the governor's words, the bank drafted the law and it passed in one day. Then Delaware
🚧 The toll booth: why cash payers often chip in for card rewards (one Fed study; the card industry disputes it)
📢 Today: a 10% cap on card interest is back in the news. It has been tried before

💬 Did you know your card's rules probably come from a state you've never been to? Yes or no.

snippet.title: Bank of America Bought Countrywide's Past | The Rules of the Game
snippet.description: In July 2008, Bank of America completed its purchase of Countrywide, a home lender, and paid with its own shares, worth about 4.2 billion dollars. Years before, Countrywide had sold big groups of its home loans, and in the contracts for those loan sales it promised that each loan was made under its written lending rules. Investors who held bonds paid from those loans later said many loans broke those rules. In June 2011, Bank of America and Countrywide signed one agreement to pay 8.5 billion dollars to settle the investors' claims, about twice the purchase price, and a New York court approved the settlement in 2015. Buying a company changes who owns it, not what the company promised. #MergersAndAcquisitions #CorporateLaw #BankOfAmerica

snippet.title: The bank, not Visa, keeps the biggest cut of the credit card swipe fee
snippet.description:
A $100 dinner on a premium rewards card sends $2.60 to the bank. On a big bank debit card: 27 cents. Same table, same bill.
Visa sets that fee, but it does not keep it. Interchange goes to the bank that issued the card. For scale, Visa's whole fiscal 2026 revenue, worldwide, was $45.9 billion, while swipe fees on Visa and Mastercard credit cards in the US alone were about $118.8 billion in 2025, by industry data. American stores paid about $198 billion in card fees in 2025 (all card processing fees, about 1.59% of purchases). Most stores charge one price however you pay, so the fee sits in the shelf price. In Europe the bank's cut on consumer credit cards has been capped at 0.3% by law since 2015, about 30 cents on $100; Visa's US premium rewards store rate is 2.30% plus 10 cents, $2.40 on $100 by our math. A 2010 Boston Fed study estimated that each cash household pays about $149 a year toward card users. Visa and Mastercard have agreed, in a merchant settlement, to cut the average credit interchange rate by 0.10 point for five years, a dime on $100; a judge gave the deal preliminary approval in June 2026 and the final hearing was set for November 16, 2026.
